question: Adult BLS compression-to-ventilation ratio with 2 rescuers:
explanation:
• For adults the compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30:2 with either one or two rescuers, until an advanced airway is placed.
• 15:2 is the two-rescuer ratio for infants and children, not adults, and 5:1 was withdrawn from the guidelines in 2005.
• Once an advanced airway is in situ, compressions become continuous at 100-120/min with one breath every 6 seconds.
citation: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and ECC (2020)

question: Adult compression depth (approx):
options: A. 1 inch
B. At least 2 inches (5 cm)
C. 3 cm only
D. As shallow as possible
explanation:
• Adult chest compressions must be at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep, and not more than 2.4 inches (6 cm), delivered at 100-120 per minute with full recoil between compressions.
• 1 inch or 3 cm is too shallow to generate the coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure needed to sustain the brain and myocardium.
• Deliberately shallow compressions are never correct; the depth limit exists only to avoid rib and visceral injury, not to justify under-compressing.
citation: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and ECC (2020)

question: Rule of Nines: adult anterior trunk is about:
explanation:
• In the adult Rule of Nines the trunk is 36% of body surface area, divided as 18% anterior and 18% posterior.
• 9% applies to each upper limb and to the head and neck, while each lower limb is 18%.
• 36% is the whole trunk (front plus back), so it overstates the anterior surface alone, and 27% is not a Rule of Nines value at all.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: First-line drug for anaphylaxis:
options: A. Oral antihistamine only
B. IM adrenaline (epinephrine)
C. IV beta blocker
D. Oral steroid only
explanation:
• Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh (adult dose 0.5 mg of 1:1000) is the first-line, life-saving treatment because it reverses bronchospasm, vasodilatation and capillary leak within minutes.
• Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only: they relieve urticaria or reduce late-phase reactions but act far too slowly to treat airway obstruction or shock.
• Beta blockers are contraindicated because they oppose the action of adrenaline and can deepen hypotension and bronchospasm.
citation: World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidance (2020 update)

question: Typical adult Hb lower limit (female approx):
options: A. 10 g/dL
B. 12 g/dL
C. 14 g/dL
D. 8 g/dL
explanation:
• WHO defines anaemia in non-pregnant adult women as haemoglobin below 12 g/dL, so 12 g/dL is the accepted lower limit of normal.
• The corresponding cut-off is 13 g/dL for adult men and 11 g/dL in pregnancy.
• 10 g/dL and 8 g/dL already represent mild-to-moderate and severe anaemia respectively, while 14 g/dL lies comfortably inside the normal female range rather than at its floor.
citation: WHO, Haemoglobin Concentrations for the Diagnosis of Anaemia and Assessment of Severity (2011)

question: Open fracture priority includes:
options: A. Immediate ROM exercises
B. Cover with sterile dressing, immobilize, urgent care
C. Massage the wound
D. Apply heat
explanation:
• An open (compound) fracture is a surgical emergency: control bleeding, cover the wound with a sterile dressing to limit contamination, immobilise the limb in the position found, and arrange urgent transfer for debridement, antibiotics and tetanus prophylaxis.
• Range-of-motion exercises would displace the bone ends, increase bleeding and risk neurovascular injury.
• Massaging the wound drives contamination deeper, and heat increases bleeding and swelling; cold and immobilisation, not heat, are used in acute fracture care.
citation: St John Ambulance / St Andrew's First Aid / British Red Cross, First Aid Manual, 11th ed. (2021)

question: Respiratory acidosis shows:
options: A. Low CO2
B. High CO2 with acidic pH
C. High HCO3 with alkalemia
D. Always normal pH
explanation:
• Respiratory acidosis is caused by alveolar hypoventilation, so carbon dioxide is retained (PaCO2 above 45 mmHg) and the pH falls below 7.35.
• A low CO2 with a raised pH describes respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, and a high bicarbonate with alkalaemia is metabolic alkalosis.
• The pH may drift back toward normal once the kidneys compensate by retaining bicarbonate, but it is never invariably normal, which rules out the last option.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: Shockable rhythms in cardiac arrest include:
options: A. Asystole
B. VF and pulseless VT
C. PEA
D. Bradycardia only
explanation:
• Only ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are shockable, because defibrillation depolarises the myocardium simultaneously and allows an organised rhythm to resume.
• Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are non-shockable and are managed with high-quality CPR, adrenaline every 3-5 minutes and correction of reversible causes.
• Bradycardia with a pulse is treated with atropine, chronotropic infusion or pacing, never with defibrillation.
citation: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and ECC (2020)

question: Clinical pathology Q9: Platelet count very low increases risk of:
options: A. Thrombosis
B. Bleeding
C. Hypernatremia
D. Metabolic alkalosis
explanation:
• Platelets form the primary haemostatic plug, so a very low count causes bleeding: petechiae, purpura, bleeding gums, epistaxis and, when severe, gastrointestinal or intracranial haemorrhage.
• Thrombosis is the opposite problem and follows platelet excess or activation, not a low count.
• Serum sodium and acid-base balance are regulated by the kidneys and lungs, so hypernatraemia and metabolic alkalosis have no causal link to the platelet count.
citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14th ed. (2018)

question: A 6-month-old infant suddenly stops feeding, cannot cry or cough and is turning blue. What is the correct first-aid sequence?
options: A. Five abdominal thrusts, as given to an adult
B. A blind finger sweep of the mouth to hook out the object
C. Five back blows followed by five chest thrusts, repeated until the object is expelled
D. Hold the infant upside down by the ankles and shake
explanation: For a choking infant with complete obstruction, five back blows delivered with the infant prone and head-down, alternating with five chest thrusts using two fingers over the lower sternum, generate enough pressure to expel the object without injuring the abdominal organs. Abdominal thrusts are the tempting answer because they are correct for adults and for children over one year, but an infant's liver is relatively large and poorly protected by the rib cage and can be lacerated. A blind finger sweep may push the object further down and is never performed.
topic: Choking - Foreign Body Airway Obstruction in Infants
citation: AHA Guidelines 2020 for CPR and ECC - Pediatric Basic Life Support

question: A man has a deep forearm laceration from broken glass and is bleeding briskly. What is the first action of the first-aider?
options: A. Apply firm direct pressure over the wound with a clean pad and raise the limb
B. Apply a tourniquet above the elbow straight away
C. Apply ice packs over the wound to constrict the vessels
D. Wash the wound under running water and wait for the bleeding to settle
explanation: Firm, sustained direct pressure over the bleeding point with a clean pad, with the limb elevated, controls the great majority of external bleeding and is the first step in every bleeding-control protocol. A tourniquet is the tempting answer, but it is reserved for life-threatening limb bleeding that direct pressure and a pressure dressing have failed to control, because it renders the whole limb ischaemic. Ice does not stop arterial or venous bleeding, and washing the wound only flushes away the clot that is forming.
citation: AHA and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid 2020 - Control of Bleeding

question: A woman spills boiling tea over her forearm. What is the correct immediate first aid for the scald?
options: A. Apply ice cubes directly to the burnt skin
B. Cool the area under cool running tap water for about 20 minutes
C. Apply toothpaste or ghee to soothe the skin
D. Deroof the blisters and paint the area with antiseptic
explanation: Cool running tap water for about 20 minutes, begun as soon as possible after the injury, limits the depth of the burn, relieves pain and reduces the need for grafting, while the rest of the body is kept covered to prevent hypothermia. Ice is the tempting choice because it feels more effective, but direct ice causes intense vasoconstriction and a cold injury that deepens the burn. Toothpaste, ghee and similar household applications trap heat, introduce infection and have to be scrubbed off later, and intact blisters should be left undisturbed.
citation: MoHFW National Programme for Prevention and Management of Burn Injuries - First Aid in Burns

question: A farmer is bitten on the calf by a snake while working in his field. Which first-aid measure should be taken before he reaches hospital?
options: A. Apply a tight arterial tourniquet above the bite
B. Incise the bite and suck out the venom
C. Rub the site with a chemical or apply a heated object
D. Reassure him, immobilise the bitten limb with a splint in a neutral position and transport him urgently
explanation: The national protocol is summarised as 'Do it R.I.G.H.T.': Reassure the victim, Immobilise the limb as though for a fracture and without any compression, Get to hospital, and Tell the doctor of any developing symptoms, because splinting slows the movement of venom into the systemic circulation while antivenom is arranged. A tourniquet is the tempting traditional answer, but arterial tourniquets cause limb ischaemia and gangrene and can deliver a sudden bolus of venom when released. Incision and suction remove almost no venom while adding bleeding and infection, which is particularly dangerous after a viper bite.

question: An adult is pulled unresponsive and not breathing from a village pond. How does resuscitation differ from standard adult basic life support?
options: A. Give five initial rescue breaths before starting chest compressions
B. Begin with 30 chest compressions exactly as for a collapse of cardiac origin
C. Give abdominal thrusts first to expel water from the lungs
D. Hold the victim head-down to drain the water before starting anything
explanation: Drowning causes cardiac arrest through hypoxia, so ventilation takes priority and five initial rescue breaths are given before the first cycle of chest compressions. Starting with compressions is the tempting answer because that is correct for the far commoner arrest of cardiac origin, where the blood is still oxygenated at the moment of collapse; in drowning the blood is already desaturated and compressions alone simply circulate hypoxic blood. Attempts to drain water by abdominal thrusts or head-down positioning waste time and provoke regurgitation and aspiration.
citation: European Resuscitation Council Guidelines - Cardiac Arrest in Special Circumstances (Drowning)

question: A construction worker collapses on a hot afternoon with a core temperature of 41 degrees Celsius, confusion and hot dry skin. What is the priority first-aid measure?
options: A. Give oral paracetamol and let him rest in the shade
B. Move him into the shade, remove excess clothing and begin rapid external cooling while arranging urgent transfer
C. Cover him with a blanket to prevent shivering
D. Make him drink a litre of ORS immediately
explanation: Heat stroke is an emergency in which outcome depends on how fast the core temperature falls, so the priority is shade, removal of clothing, cold water or ice packs to the neck, axillae and groin, and fanning, all while urgent transfer is organised. Paracetamol is the tempting answer because the patient is hot, but antipyretics act on a hypothalamic set point that is not raised in heat stroke; the hyperthermia results from failed heat loss, so they do not work and may add liver injury. Oral fluids are unsafe in a confused patient because of the risk of aspiration.
citation: MoHFW National Action Plan for Heat Related Illnesses

question: An adult is found unresponsive but breathing normally, with no suspicion of spinal injury. In which position should the first-aider place him?
options: A. Supine with a pillow under the head
B. Head-down (Trendelenburg) position
C. Lateral recovery position
D. Prone with the face turned to one side
explanation: The lateral recovery position keeps the airway open and allows saliva, blood or vomit to drain out of the mouth, which is the main threat to an unresponsive person who is still breathing. Supine with a pillow is tempting because it looks comfortable and is how a patient is nursed in bed, but the tongue falls back against the pharynx and any vomit is aspirated. A head-down position adds nothing here and impairs breathing, and the prone position makes it hard to watch the airway or to turn the victim quickly if CPR becomes necessary.
citation: Indian Red Cross Society First Aid Manual - Unconsciousness

question: A man has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at a bus stop. What should the bystander do?
options: A. Force a cloth-wrapped spoon between the teeth to stop him biting his tongue
B. Hold the arms and legs firmly to stop the jerking
C. Splash cold water on the face to bring him round
D. Clear the surroundings, cushion the head, note the time and turn him on his side once the jerking stops
explanation: Seizure first aid is protective rather than interventional: move hard objects away, put something soft under the head, loosen tight clothing, time the seizure and place the person in the lateral position once the convulsion ends so that secretions drain freely. Putting an object in the mouth is the classic tempting mistake, but the tongue cannot be swallowed and forcing anything between clenched teeth breaks teeth, injures the mouth and endangers the rescuer's fingers. Restraining the limbs causes fractures and dislocations and does not shorten the seizure.

question: A workman is found lying motionless while still gripping a live electrical cable. What must the rescuer do first?
options: A. Switch off the mains supply, or push the victim clear with a dry non-conducting object, before touching him
B. Pull the victim away by the hand at once to shorten the contact time
C. Pour water over the cable to cool it and break the current
D. Start chest compressions where he lies, while he is still in contact with the cable
explanation: The current is still flowing, so the supply must be isolated at the mains, or the casualty separated using a dry wooden or plastic non-conductor, before any contact is made; otherwise the rescuer becomes a second casualty. Pulling him clear by hand is the instinctive and therefore tempting response, but the human body conducts electricity and the rescuer is electrocuted through the same circuit. Water conducts current and spreads the hazard, and CPR is begun only after the scene has been made safe, thereafter following the standard cardiac arrest sequence.
citation: Indian Red Cross Society First Aid Manual - Electrical Injuries
